---
title: "Build: Research Scout"
---

The 55-minute build, in four steps. Work at your own pace — the timings are guardrails, not a race.

## Step 0. Get the starter (2 min, part of scaffold time)

Clone the starter repo (or download it as a zip if you'd rather skip git):

```bash
git clone https://github.com/byu-strategy/research-scout-starter.git
cd research-scout-starter
```

*(Repo is live. It contains a README, the prompt template below, and `sample-data.json` — see the offline fallback at the bottom of this page.)*

Open the folder in VS Code (File → Open Folder), open a terminal, run `claude`.

## Step 1. Scaffold (10 min)

Paste this starter prompt into Claude Code:

```
Build a web app that searches the OpenAlex API for academic papers on a
topic and shows title, authors, venue, year, citations, DOI.
API pattern:
https://api.openalex.org/works?search=TOPIC&filter=from_publication_date:2022-01-01&sort=cited_by_count:desc
```

Approve Claude's actions as it works. When it says it's done, ask it to run the app locally and open it in your browser. Search a topic you care about. You should see real papers.

## Step 2. Iterate (25 min)

This is the divergence phase — make it yours. Pick features you'd actually use and describe them in plain English. Ideas:

1. **Publication-trend chart** — "Add a chart of publications per year for the current search. Use the OpenAlex group_by parameter: `https://api.openalex.org/works?search=TOPIC&group_by=publication_year`."
2. **Venue filter** — "Let me filter results to a specific journal or venue."
3. **Citation sort toggle** — "Add a toggle to sort by citations vs. recency."
4. **BibTeX export** — "Add a button that exports my shortlist as a BibTeX file."
5. **Saved shortlist pane** — "Let me save papers to a shortlist that persists in the browser."
6. **Compare two topics** — "Add a view that compares two search topics side by side, including their trend lines."
7. **Abstract preview** — "Show the abstract when I click a paper." (OpenAlex returns abstracts as an inverted index — tell Claude that; watch it cope.)
8. **Open-access filter** — "Add a filter for open-access papers only."
9. **Mobile layout** — "Make it look good on a phone." (You'll want this for the deploy step.)
10. **Your call** — the best feature is the one you wish existed. Describe it.

After each feature: test it, and if it's not right, say specifically what's wrong. Iteration is the workflow.

## Step 3. Deploy (10 min)

Ship it to the public internet.

1. **Push to GitHub via Claude Code.** In the Claude terminal:

   ```
   Create a new GitHub repo for this project and push the code to it.
   ```

   Claude will use the `gh` CLI; approve its steps and authenticate if prompted.

2. **Import to Vercel.** Go to [vercel.com/new](https://vercel.com/new), sign in (with GitHub), pick your new repo, click **Deploy**. Defaults are fine.

3. **Get your URL.** In ~1 minute Vercel gives you a live `*.vercel.app` URL. Open it **on your phone**. That's your research tool, on the public internet, built in under an hour.

Stuck on deploy? Ask Claude Code: "Walk me through deploying this to Vercel." It knows.

## Step 4. Reflect (5 min)

Before the group debrief, jot answers to one question: **what did you decide, and what did AI decide?** Bring your list — it's the raw material for the [debrief](22-building-debrief.qmd).

::: {.callout-warning}
## Offline fallback (if the wifi or the API dies)

The starter repo bundles `sample-data.json` — a 37-paper corpus on AI and knowledge work. If live requests fail, tell Claude Code: "The API is unreachable — load results from sample-data.json instead." The whole build works offline; switching back to the live API later is a one-line change.
:::
